title: Chapter 14 — Of Prerogative
paragraphs: Where the legislative and executive power are in different hands (as they are in all moderated monarchies and well-framed governments), the good of the society requires that various things be left to the discretion of the one who has the executive power. The legislators are not able to foresee everything that may be useful to the community and provide for it by laws. So the executor of the laws, having the power in his hands, has a right by the common law of nature to use it for the good of the society in many cases where the municipal law has given no direction, until the legislative can conveniently be assembled to provide for it. There are many things which the law can in no way provide for, and those must necessarily be left to the discretion of whoever has the executive power in his hands, to be ordered by him as the public good and advantage require. Indeed, it is fitting that the laws themselves should in some cases give way to the executive power, or rather to this fundamental law of nature and government: namely, that as far as possible all the members of the society are to be preserved. For many accidents may happen in which a strict and rigid observance of the laws may do harm (for example, refusing to pull down an innocent man’s house to stop a fire when the house next to it is burning). And a man may sometimes come within the reach of the law, which makes no distinction between persons, through an action that may deserve reward and pardon. So it is fitting that the ruler should have a power, in many cases, to soften the severity of the law and to pardon some offenders. For since the end of government is the preservation of all, as far as possible, even the guilty are to be spared where this can do no harm to the innocent.

This power to act according to discretion, for the public good, without the prescription of the law, and sometimes even against it, is what is called prerogative. In some governments the lawmaking power is not always in being, and it is usually too numerous, and so too slow, for the speed that execution requires. It is also impossible to foresee, and so to provide for by laws, all the accidents and necessities that may concern the public, or to make laws that will do no harm if they are executed with inflexible rigour on all occasions and upon all persons who may come in their way. For these reasons a latitude is left to the executive power to do many things by its own choice which the laws do not prescribe.

As long as this power is employed for the benefit of the community, and in keeping with the trust and ends of the government, it is undoubted prerogative and is never questioned. The people are very seldom, if ever, scrupulous or fussy on this point. They are far from examining prerogative as long as it is employed to any tolerable degree for the use it was meant for, that is, for the good of the people, and not plainly against it. But if a dispute arises between the executive power and the people about something claimed as a prerogative, the question will easily be decided by whether the exercise of that prerogative tends to the good or the harm of the people.

It is easy to imagine that in the infancy of governments, when commonwealths differed little from families in the number of their people, they also differed little from them in the number of their laws. The governors were like fathers to them, watching over them for their good, and so the government was almost all prerogative. A few established laws served the purpose, and the discretion and care of the ruler supplied the rest. But when error or flattery persuaded weak princes to use this power for private ends of their own, and not for the public good, the people were obliged to have prerogative defined by express laws on those points where they found it working to their disadvantage. So the people found it necessary to declare limits on prerogative in cases which they and their ancestors had left, with the widest latitude, to the wisdom of those princes who made nothing but a right use of it, that is, who used it for the good of their people.

So those who say that the people have encroached on the prerogative when they have had any part of it defined by positive laws have a very wrong notion of government. In doing so the people have not taken from the prince anything that rightly belonged to him. They have only declared that the power they left indefinitely in his hands, or his ancestors’, to be exercised for their good, was not something they intended him to have when he used it otherwise. For since the end of government is the good of the community, whatever alterations are made in it that tend toward that end cannot be an encroachment on anybody, because nobody in government can have a right that tends toward any other end. The only encroachments are those that harm or hinder the public good. Those who say otherwise speak as if the prince had an interest distinct and separate from the good of the community, and was not made for it. That is the root and source from which almost all the evils and disorders that happen in kingly governments spring. And indeed, if that is so, the people under his government are not a society of rational creatures who have entered into a community for their mutual good. They are not people who have set rulers over themselves to guard and promote that good. Instead they are to be regarded as a herd of inferior creatures under the dominion of a master, who keeps them and works them for his own pleasure or profit. If men were so devoid of reason, and so brutish, as to enter into society on such terms, prerogative might indeed be what some men would like it to be: an arbitrary power to do things harmful to the people.

But a rational creature cannot be supposed, when he is free, to put himself into subjection to another for his own harm (although, where he finds a good and wise ruler, he may not perhaps think it either necessary or useful to set precise limits to his power in all things). So prerogative can be nothing but the people’s permitting their rulers to do various things by their own free choice, where the law was silent, and sometimes even against the direct letter of the law, for the public good, together with the people’s acceptance of it when it has been done. A good prince, who is mindful of the trust placed in his hands and careful of the good of his people, cannot have too much prerogative, that is, too much power to do good. But a weak and bad prince may claim the power his predecessors exercised without the direction of the law as a prerogative belonging to him by right of his office, which he may exercise as he pleases to create or promote an interest distinct from that of the public. Such a prince gives the people occasion to claim their right and to limit that power, which they were content to allow tacitly as long as it was exercised for their good.

So anyone who looks into the history of England will find that prerogative was always largest in the hands of our wisest and best princes. The people saw that the whole tendency of their actions was the public good, and so did not contest what was done without law to that end. Or, if some human frailty or mistake appeared in small deviations from that end (for princes are only men, made like others), it was still plain that the main course of their conduct aimed at nothing but the care of the public. The people therefore, finding reason to be satisfied with these princes, accepted what they did whenever they acted without the letter of the law or contrary to it, and, without the least complaint, let them enlarge their prerogative as they pleased. They judged rightly that in this the princes did nothing to harm their laws, since they acted in accordance with the foundation and end of all laws, the public good.

Such god-like princes did indeed have some title to arbitrary power, by the argument that would prove absolute monarchy the best government, as the one by which God himself governs the universe: because such kings share in his wisdom and goodness. On this is founded the saying that the reigns of good princes have always been the most dangerous to the liberties of their people. For their successors, managing the government with different ideas, would take the actions of those good rulers as precedents and make them the standard of their own prerogative, as if what had been done only for the good of the people gave them a right to do the same for the harm of the people, if they so pleased. This has often caused conflict, and sometimes public disorder, before the people could recover their original right and have it declared that this was not prerogative, as it truly never was. For it is impossible that anybody in the society should ever have a right to do the people harm, although it is quite possible, and reasonable, that the people should not try to set any limits to the prerogative of those kings or rulers who did not themselves overstep the bounds of the public good. For prerogative is nothing but the power of doing public good without a rule.

The power of calling parliaments in England, as to their exact time, place, and duration, is certainly a prerogative of the king, but still with this trust: that it is to be used for the good of the nation, as the needs of the times and the variety of occasions require. It is impossible to foresee which place will always be the fittest for them to assemble in, and what the best season will be, so the choice of these was left with the executive power, to be made in the way that might best serve the public good and best suit the ends of parliaments.

In this matter of prerogative the old question will be asked: but who shall be judge of when this power is being used rightly? I answer: between an executive power in being with such a prerogative, and a legislative that depends on his will for its convening, there can be no judge on earth. Nor can there be one between the legislative and the people, should either the executive or the legislative, once they have the power in their hands, plan or set about enslaving or destroying them. In this case, as in all other cases where they have no judge on earth, the people have no other remedy but to appeal to heaven. For the rulers, in such attempts, are exercising a power the people never put into their hands (since the people can never be supposed to consent that anybody should rule over them for their harm), and so they are doing what they have no right to do. And where the body of the people, or any single man, is deprived of their right, or is subjected to the exercise of a power without right, and has no appeal on earth, they have a liberty to appeal to heaven whenever they judge the cause to be of sufficient importance. Therefore, although the people cannot be judge in the sense of having, by the constitution of that society, any superior power to decide the case and pass an effective sentence, they have nevertheless, by a law prior and superior to all the positive laws of men, reserved to themselves that ultimate decision which belongs to all mankind where there is no appeal on earth: namely, to judge whether they have just cause to make their appeal to heaven. And they cannot part with this judgment, because it is beyond a man’s power to submit himself to another so far as to give him a liberty to destroy him. God and nature never allow a man to abandon himself so far as to neglect his own preservation; and since he cannot take away his own life, neither can he give another the power to take it. Nor should anyone think that this lays a perpetual foundation for disorder. For it does not come into operation until the inconvenience is so great that the majority feel it, are weary of it, and find it necessary to have it put right. But the executive power, or wise princes, never need come into danger of this; and it is the thing, above all others, that they most need to avoid, as the most perilous of all.
